question.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $k(3-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=4\,m/s$ at the origin and has velocity $v=2\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when its displacement is $2\,m,$ find the maximum velocity of the particle.
question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14273713/assets/2d768dd32288c71332e81b0f72aa2652c19a7c80fed6751abea5ced383e6848f.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k(3-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k(3-x).
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}k(3-x) & =0 \\ 3-x & =0 \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=3\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,3)$ | $3$ | $(3,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $2$ |  | $4$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $k>0$ | $0$ | $-k<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=3\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k(3-x).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int k(3-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(3x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(3x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =k(3(0)-\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2})+C \\ C & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(3x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+8.
$$

Also, since $v=2\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when $x=2\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(3x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+8 \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{6})^{2} & =k(3(2)-\frac{1}{2}{(2)}^{2})+8 \\ 12 & =4k+8 \\ 4k & =4 \\ k & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =1(3x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+8 \\ {v}^{2} & =6x-{x}^{2}+16 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{-{x}^{2}+6x+16}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+6x+16}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(3)=\sqrt{-(3)^{2}+6(3)+16}=5\,m/s
$$
